claim: Providing knowledge of results on only about half of practice trials, or fading it out, produced retention equal to or better than feedback on every trial.
title: Reduced Frequency of Knowledge of Results Enhances Motor Skill Learning

claim: Frequent extrinsic feedback guides performance during practice but can degrade learning by preventing the learner from developing intrinsic error-detection.
title: Knowledge of Results and Motor Learning: A Review and Critical Reappraisal

claim: Skilled typists slowed after their own keystroke errors even when the screen was corrected, showing error detection at the motor level independent of the display.
title: Cognitive Illusions of Authorship Reveal Hierarchical Error Detection in Skilled Typists

claim: Removing visual feedback of the typed text had little effect on error detection but greatly reduced error correction.
title: The role of visual feedback in detecting and correcting typing errors: A signal detection approach

claim: In a dataset of 136 million keystrokes, typing speed was predicted mainly by inter-key intervals of letter pairs typed with different hands or fingers and by rollover, rather than by single-key identity.
title: Observations on Typing from 136 Million Keystrokes

claim: Self-taught typists reached speeds comparable to trained touch typists; speed was predicted by consistent finger-to-key mapping rather than the number of fingers used.
title: How We Type: Movement Strategies and Performance in Everyday Typing

claim: Measuring an enjoyable activity increased how much people engaged in it but decreased their enjoyment and subsequent voluntary engagement.
title: The Hidden Cost of Personal Quantification

claim: Postal workers trained in one one-hour session per day learned to type in fewer total hours than groups trained in longer or more frequent sessions.
title: The Influence of Length and Frequency of Training Session on the Rate of Learning to Type

claim: Part-task training transferred positively for tasks whose components were separable and was neutral or harmful where components were highly interdependent.
title: Effectiveness of Part-Task Training and Increasing-Difficulty Training Strategies: A Meta-Analysis Approach

claim: Skilled typing is controlled by two nested loops: an outer loop that produces words and an inner loop that produces keystrokes, with the inner loop informationally encapsulated from the outer.
title: Hierarchical Control of Cognitive Processes: The Case for Skilled Typewriting

claim: Identifier count, line length and punctuation density are among the strongest features predicting lower human-rated code readability.
title: Learning a Metric for Code Readability

claim: Keyboard layout optimisation is formulated as an assignment problem whose objective sums bigram frequency times key-pair movement cost.
title: Improvements to Keyboard Optimization with Integer Programming

claim: Real-world code completions differ from synthetic benchmarks and developers rely on completion most for long identifiers.
title: When Code Completion Fails: A Case Study on Real-World Completions

claim: In a large study of an action RPG, both no juiciness and extreme juiciness reduced play time, player experience and performance relative to medium and high juiciness.
title: The effects of juiciness in an action RPG

claim: Visual embellishments that carry no gameplay information improved perceived appeal and sense of agency in player experience studies.
title: Juicy Game Design: Understanding the Impact of Visual Embellishments on Player Experience

claim: A version of a game with juicy audio effects produced higher reported presence than the same game without them.
title: That Sound's Juicy! Exploring Juicy Audio Effects in Video Games

claim: Auditory feedback such as error sonification mapped to pitch supports motor learning and its benefits persist better than concurrent visual feedback when feedback is withdrawn.
title: Augmented visual, auditory, haptic, and multimodal feedback in motor learning: A review

claim: Synchronising game events with music affected performance and experience in a VR rhythm game, mediated by whether players consciously perceived the synchronisation.
title: The Effect of Auditory-Motor Synchronization in Exergames on the Example of the VR Rhythm Game BeatSaber

claim: Near-miss outcomes in a gambling task were rated less pleasant than full misses yet increased the desire to continue and activated reward-related brain regions.
title: Gambling Near-Misses Enhance Motivation to Gamble and Recruit Win-Related Brain Circuitry

claim: Fast-tempo music increased speed but also increased errors in a driving game relative to slower or no music.
title: The effects of music on time perception and performance of a driving game

claim: Dynamic difficulty adjustment techniques aim to keep players in a flow channel by adjusting challenge in real time based on observed performance.
title: Dynamic Difficulty Adjustment (DDA) in Computer Games: A Review

claim: Transcription typing operates on a limited eye-hand span of several characters and typing skill is unrelated to comprehension of the copied text.
title: Perceptual, Cognitive, and Motoric Aspects of Transcription Typing

claim: Typographic emphasis in written text and prosodic stress in spoken text increased detection of changed words.
title: Shallow Processing and Attention Capture in Written and Spoken Discourse

claim: In visual search, miss rates rose sharply as target prevalence fell from common to rare.
title: Rare items often missed in visual searches

claim: Humor in computer games functions to support play, including softening failure and carrying narrative, rather than as decoration.
title: A Review of Humor for Computer Games: Play, Laugh and More

claim: In a randomised trial of humorous versus plain script variants in a learning game, perceived humor and character likeability differed but completion and amount played did not.
title: Exploring players' experience of humor and snark in a grade 3-6 history practices game
authors: Gagnon, Kern, Bryant, Kinnebrew, Hoyer, Garbin, Bell

claim: A learning game whose fantasy was intrinsically integrated with its core mechanic produced better motivation and learning than a version where the same content was extrinsic to play.
title: Motivating Children to Learn Effectively: Exploring the Value of Intrinsic Integration in Educational Games

claim: Embedding a learning activity in a fantasy context with personalisation increased intrinsic motivation, engagement and learning.
title: Intrinsic Motivation and the Process of Learning: Beneficial Effects of Contextualization, Personalization, and Choice

claim: Humor arises when something is perceived as a violation that is simultaneously benign.
title: Benign Violations: Making Immoral Behavior Funny

claim: Disparagement humor is enjoyed more when it targets an out-group, and in-group targeting can be accepted when it signals shared membership rather than derogation.
title: Disparagement humor: A theoretical and empirical review of psychoanalytic, superiority, and social identity theories

claim: Intertextual jokes depend on the audience recognising the referenced text, and unrecognised references exclude the audience from the humor.
title: Intertextuality and/in political jokes

claim: Large language models generated humor rated below mid-tier human performers and weighted novelty where humans weighted empathy.
title: Assessing the Capabilities of Large Language Models in Humor: Oogiri Generation and Evaluation

claim: AI-generated jokes were judged fluent but derivative and formulaic compared with human-written humor.
title: Can AI Take a Joke, Or Make One? Evaluating Humor Generation in Large Language Models
